## The Museum of Almost

The Museum of Almost opens at 4:17 in the afternoon, in a narrow building wedged between a dry cleaner and a bakery that closed years ago.

There is no sign above the door. No ticket booth. You simply push the brass handle, and if the timing is right, the door opens.

Inside, the air smells faintly of dust, old paper, and rain that has not yet fallen.

The first exhibit is a letter begun on a train:

> My dear Maria,

The train rocks gently. Outside, fields turn gold. A man across the aisle is reading a book with a green cover, and you realize that if the train had stopped ten minutes earlier, you would have spoken to him.

The letter ends there.

In a glass case nearby is a bicycle with a crooked front wheel. Its label reads: **The Afternoon You Didn’t Learn to Ride.**

A boy stands in front of it for a long time. He does not remember anything—not the scraped knee, not the shout from behind the hedge, not the small triumphant feeling of coasting three yards. Still, when he looks at the bicycle, his knees begin to ache.

Farther down the hallway is a cup of tea gone cold.

The label explains: **You Were Going to Leave, but She Said Something Funny.**

Whoever drinks from this cup will hear the laugh, though never quite understand why it mattered.

There is a red mitten in a wooden box. A telephone number written on the margin of a newspaper. A key to a house that was never moved into. A grocery list abandoned halfway through, its remaining contents strangely urgent: soap, lemons, courage.

The museum does not collect regrets, exactly. Regret is loud and obvious, and has already been discussed enough. The museum collects the quieter things: the lives that existed for a moment before life chose a different direction.

In the central hall, there is a machine made of brass and blue glass. It does not predict the future. It shows you one possible future—the one that nearly happened.

A woman presses the lever and sees herself accepting a job in another city. She sees the apartment with two windows, the unfamiliar grocery store, the friend who becomes important in year three.

The vision is beautiful.

Then the machine clicks.

**Possibility exhausted. Please try another.**

The curator, who has never once been photographed, says this is not a machine of regrets. “It is a machine of abundance,” she explains. “Most people think only one life is available to them. But look how many rooms we pass through without entering.”

Outside, evening settles over the street. The bakery remains closed. A bus sighs at the corner. Somewhere nearby, someone is deciding whether to call an old friend.

The museum has no gift shop.

Everything people leave behind is already enough.

**The Museum of Almost**

The museum opens at 4:17... in a building between a dry cleaner and a closed bakery. No sign, door unlocked. At first glance empty, but each room holds a life that almost happened. First gallery: letter started... etc.

"The museum does not preserve what people regret, exactly. Regret is loud and has many exhibits. It preserves the quieter thing: the moment before a decision, when another self was still possible."

A boy stands before a bicycle with a crooked front wheel. Label: "The afternoon you did not learn to ride." He touches glass; remembers nothing but feels fear in knees. Office worker finds an appointment not attended, and hears rain. Someone sees red mitten in lost-and-found, etc.

At center "Hall of Near Misses." A cup of tea gone cold because conversation became important. Name on tip of tongue. A song heard through open window, no one looked up. The museum claims near-misses are not failures, but "evidence of abundance"—life branching in all directions, most unseen. That line nice.

Closing: late afternoon, door wants closing. "If you are ever standing at a crossroads, remember: the road not taken is not a road that disappeared. It is still there, humming behind the hedge, waiting to be a story." That's somewhat conventional but okay. Maybe "The museum has no gift shop. The things people leave behind are already enough." Nice.
